In [[mathematics]], the '''Rudin–Shapiro sequence''', also known as the '''Golay–Rudin–Shapiro sequence''', is an infinite 2-[[automatic sequence]] named after [[Marcel J.E. Golay|Marcel Golay]], [[Harold S. Shapiro]], and [[Walter Rudin]], who investigated its properties.<ref name=bm>{{cite journal|title=A Case Study in Mathematical Research: The Golay–Rudin–Shapiro Sequence|author=John Brillhart and Patrick Morton, winners of a 1997 [[Lester R. Ford Award]]|journal=Amer. Math. Monthly|year=1996|volume=103|issue=10 |pages=854–869|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/a-case-study-in-mathematical-research-the-golay-rudin-shapiro-sequence|doi=10.2307/2974610|jstor=2974610 }}</ref>

== Definition ==
Each term of the Rudin–Shapiro sequence is either <math>1</math> or <math>-1</math>. If the binary expansion of <math>n</math> is given by
: <math>n = \sum_{k \ge 0} \epsilon_k(n) 2^k,</math>
then let
: <math>u_n = \sum_{k \ge 0} \epsilon_k(n)\epsilon_{k+1}(n).</math>
(So <math>u_n</math> is the number of times the block 11 appears in the binary expansion of <math>n</math>.)

The Rudin–Shapiro sequence <math>(r_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> is then defined by
: <math>r_n = (-1)^{u_n}.</math>

Thus <math>r_n = 1</math> if <math>u_n</math> is even and <math>r_n = -1</math> if <math>u_n</math> is odd.<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=Rudin-ShapiroSequence|title=Rudin–Shapiro Sequence}}</ref><ref name=PF42/><ref>Everest et al (2003) p.234</ref>

The sequence <math>u_n</math> is known as the complete Rudin–Shapiro sequence, and starting at <math>n = 0</math>, its first few terms are:
: 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, ... {{OEIS|A014081}}
and the corresponding terms <math>r_n</math> of the Rudin–Shapiro sequence are:
: +1, +1, +1, &minus;1, +1, +1, &minus;1, +1, +1, +1, +1, &minus;1, &minus;1, &minus;1, +1, &minus;1, ... {{OEIS|A020985}}

For example, <math>u_6 = 1</math> and <math>r_6 = -1</math> because the binary representation of 6 is 110, which contains one occurrence of 11; whereas <math>u_7 = 2</math> and <math>r_7 = 1</math> because the binary representation of 7 is 111, which contains two (overlapping) occurrences of 11.

== Historical motivation ==

The Rudin–Shapiro sequence was introduced independently by Golay,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Golay |first1=M.J.E. |title=Multi-slit spectrometry |journal= Journal of the Optical Society of America|date=1949 |volume=39 |issue=437–444|pages=437–444 |doi=10.1364/JOSA.39.000437 |pmid=18152021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Golay |first1=M.J.E. |title=Static multislit spectrometry and its application to the panoramic display of infrared spectra. |journal= Journal of the Optical Society of America|date=1951 |volume=41 |issue=7 |pages=468–472|doi=10.1364/JOSA.41.000468 |pmid=14851129 }}</ref> Rudin,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rudin |first1=W. |title=Some theorems on Fourier coefficients. |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1959 |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=855–859|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1959-0116184-5 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and Shapiro.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shapiro |first1=H.S. |title=Extremal problems for polynomials and power series. |journal=Master's Thesis, MIT. |date=1952}}</ref> The following is a description of Rudin's motivation. In [[Fourier analysis]], one is often concerned with the [[Lp space|<math>L^2</math> norm]] of a [[measurable function]] <math>f \colon [0,2\pi) \to [0,2\pi) </math>. This norm is defined by
: <math>
||f||_2 = \left(\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} |f(t)|^2\,\mathrm{d}t\right)^{1/2}.</math>

One can prove that for any sequence <math>(a_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> with each <math>a_n</math> in <math>\{1,-1\}</math>,
: <math>\sup_{x \in \R} \left|\sum_{0 \le n < N} a_n e^{inx}\right| \ge \left|\left|\sum_{0 \le n < N} a_n e^{inx}\right|\right|_2 = \sqrt{N}.</math>

Moreover, for almost every sequence <math>(a_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> with each <math>a_n</math> is in <math>\{-1,1\}</math>,
: <math>
\sup_{x \in \R} \left|\sum_{0 \le n < N} a_n e^{inx} \right| = O(\sqrt{N \log N}).</math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Salem |first1=R. |last2=Zygmund |first2=A. |author-link2=Antoni Zygmund |title=Some properties of trigonometric series whose terms have random signs. |journal=[[Acta Mathematica]] |date=1954 |volume=91 |pages=245–301|doi=10.1007/BF02393433 |s2cid=122999383 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

However, the Rudin–Shapiro sequence <math>(r_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> satisfies a tighter bound:<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 78–79</ref> there exists a constant <math>C > 0</math> such that
: <math>
\sup_{x \in \R} \left|\sum_{0 \le n < N} r_n e^{inx} \right| \le C\sqrt{N}.</math>

It is conjectured that one can take <math>C = \sqrt{6}</math>,<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 122</ref> but while it is known that <math>C \ge \sqrt{6}</math>,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brillhart |first1=J. |last2=Morton |first2=P. |title=Über Summen von Rudin–Shapiroschen Koeffizienten. |journal=[[Illinois Journal of Mathematics]] |date=1978 |volume=22 |pages=126–148|doi=10.1215/ijm/1256048841 |doi-access=free }}</ref> the best published upper bound is currently <math>C \le (2+\sqrt{2})\sqrt{3/5}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Saffari |first1=B. |title=Une fonction extrémale liée à la suite de Rudin–Shapiro. |journal=[[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris]] |date=1986 |volume=303 |pages=97–100}}</ref> Let <math>P_n</math> be the ''n''-th [[Shapiro polynomials|Shapiro polynomial]]. Then, when <math>N = 2^n-1</math>, the above inequality gives a bound on <math>\sup_{x \in \R} |P_n(e^{ix})|</math>. More recently, bounds have also been given for the magnitude of the coefficients of <math>|P_n(z)|^2</math> where <math>|z| = 1</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Allouche |first1=J.-P. |last2=Choi |first2=S. |last3=Denise |first3=A. |last4=Erdélyi |first4=T. |last5=Saffari |first5=B. |title=Bounds on Autocorrelation Coefficients of Rudin-Shapiro Polynomials |journal=Analysis Mathematica |date=2019 |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=705–726|doi=10.1007/s10476-019-0003-4 |arxiv=1901.06832 |s2cid=119168430 }}</ref>

Shapiro arrived at the sequence because the polynomials 
: <math>P_n(z) = \sum_{i=0}^{2^n-1} r_i z^i</math>
where <math>(r_i)_{i \ge 0}</math> is the Rudin–Shapiro sequence, have absolute value bounded on the complex unit circle by <math>2^{\frac{n+1}{2}}</math>. This is discussed in more detail in the article on [[Shapiro polynomials]]. Golay's motivation was similar, although he was concerned with applications to [[spectroscopy]] and published in an optics journal.

== Properties ==
The Rudin–Shapiro sequence can be generated by a 4-state [[finite-state machine|automaton]] accepting binary representations of non-negative integers as input.<ref>[http://www.emis.de/journals/SLC/opapers/s30allouche.pdf Finite automata and arithmetic], Jean-Paul Allouche</ref> The sequence is therefore 2-automatic, so by [[Automatic sequence#Substitution|Cobham's little theorem]] there exists a [[Free monoid#Morphisms|2-uniform morphism]] <math>\varphi</math> with fixed point <math>w</math> and a coding <math>\tau</math> such that <math>r = \tau(w)</math>, where <math>r</math> is the Rudin–Shapiro sequence. However, the Rudin–Shapiro sequence cannot be expressed as the fixed point of some uniform morphism alone.<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 192</ref>

There is a [[recursive definition]]<ref name=PF42>Pytheas Fogg (2002) p.42</ref>
: <math>
\begin{cases} 
r_{2n} & = r_n  \\
r_{2n+1} & = (-1)^n r_n 
\end{cases}</math>

The values of the terms ''r''<sub>''n''</sub> and ''u''<sub>''n''</sub> in the Rudin–Shapiro sequence can be found recursively as follows. If ''n'' = ''m''·2<sup>''k''</sup> where ''m'' is odd then
: <math>u_n =
\begin{cases} 
u_{(m-1)/4} & \text{if } m \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \\
u_{(m-1)/2} + 1 & \text{if } m \equiv 3 \pmod 4
\end{cases}</math>
: <math>r_n =
\begin{cases} 
r_{(m-1)/4} & \text{if } m \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \\
-r_{(m-1)/2} & \text{if } m \equiv 3 \pmod 4
\end{cases}</math>

Thus ''u''<sub>108</sub> = ''u''<sub>13</sub> + 1 = ''u''<sub>3</sub> + 1 = ''u''<sub>1</sub> + 2 = ''u''<sub>0</sub> + 2 = 2, which can be verified by observing that the binary representation of 108, which is 1101100, contains two sub-strings 11. And so ''r''<sub>108</sub> = (&minus;1)<sup>2</sup> = +1.

A 2-uniform morphism <math>\varphi</math> that requires a coding <math>\tau</math>  to generate the Rudin-Shapiro sequence is the following:<math display="block">\begin{align}
\varphi: a&\to ab\\
b&\to ac\\
c&\to db\\
d&\to dc
\end{align}</math>    <math display="block">\begin{align}
\tau: a&\to 1\\
b&\to 1\\
c&\to -1\\
d&\to -1
\end{align}</math>

The Rudin–Shapiro word +1 +1 +1 &minus;1 +1 +1 &minus;1 +1 +1 +1 +1 &minus;1 &minus;1 &minus;1 +1 &minus;1 ..., which is created by concatenating the terms of the Rudin–Shapiro sequence, is a fixed point of the morphism or [[string substitution]] rules
: +1 +1  '''→'''  +1 +1 +1 &minus;1
: +1 &minus;1  '''→'''  +1 +1 &minus;1 +1
: &minus;1 +1  '''→'''  &minus;1 &minus;1 +1 &minus;1
: &minus;1 &minus;1  '''→'''  &minus;1 &minus;1 &minus;1 +1
as follows:
: +1 +1 '''→''' +1 +1 +1 &minus;1 '''→''' +1 +1 +1 &minus;1 +1 +1 &minus;1 +1 '''→''' +1 +1 +1 &minus;1 +1 +1 &minus;1 +1 +1 +1 +1 &minus;1 &minus;1 &minus;1 +1 &minus;1 ...

It can be seen from the morphism rules that the Rudin–Shapiro string contains at most four consecutive +1s and at most four consecutive &minus;1s.

The sequence of partial sums of the Rudin–Shapiro sequence, defined by
: <math>s_n = \sum_{k=0}^n r_k \, ,</math>
with values
: 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 6, 5, 4, 5, 4, ... {{OEIS|A020986}}
can be shown to satisfy the inequality
: <math>\sqrt{\frac{3}{5} n} < s_n < \sqrt{6n} \text{ for } n \ge 1 \, .</math><ref name=bm />

Let <math>(s_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> denote the Rudin–Shapiro sequence on <math>\{0,1\}</math>, in which case <math>s_n</math> is the number, modulo 2, of occurrences (possibly overlapping) of the block <math>11</math> in the base-2 expansion of <math>n</math>. Then the [[generating function]]
: <math>S(X) = \sum_{n \ge 0} s_n X^n</math>
satisfies
: <math>(1+X)^5 S(X)^2 + (1+X)^4 S(X) + X^3 = 0,</math>
making it algebraic as a formal [[power series]] over <math>\mathbb{F}_2(X)</math>.<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 352</ref> The algebraicity of <math>S(X)</math> over <math>\mathbb{F}_2(X)</math> follows from the 2-automaticity of <math>(s_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> by [[Automatic sequence#Formal power series|Christol's theorem]].

The Rudin–Shapiro sequence along squares <math>(r_{n^2})_{n \ge 0}</math> is normal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Müllner |first1=C. |title=The Rudin–Shapiro sequence and similar sequences are normal along squares. |journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics |year=2018 |volume=70 |issue=5 |pages=1096–1129|doi=10.4153/CJM-2017-053-1 |arxiv=1704.06472 |s2cid=125493369 }}</ref>

The complete Rudin–Shapiro sequence satisfies the following uniform distribution result. If <math>x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Z}</math>, then there exists <math>\alpha = \alpha(x) \in (0,1)</math> such that
: <math>\sum_{n < N} \exp(2\pi ixu_n) = O(N^{\alpha})</math>
which implies that <math>(xu_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> is uniformly distributed modulo <math>1</math> for all irrationals <math>x</math>.<ref>Allouche and Shallit p. 462–464</ref>

== Relationship with one-dimensional Ising model ==

Let the binary expansion of n be given by
: <math>n = \sum_{k \ge 0} \epsilon_k(n) 2^k</math>
where <math>\epsilon_k(n) \in \{0,1\}</math>. Recall that the complete Rudin–Shapiro sequence is defined by
: <math>u(n) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \epsilon_k(n)\epsilon_{k+1}(n).</math>

Let
: <math>\tilde{\epsilon}_k(n) = \begin{cases}
\epsilon_k(n) & \text{if } k \le N-1, \\
\epsilon_0(n)& \text{if } k = N.
\end{cases}</math>

Then let
: <math>u(n,N) = \sum_{0 \le k < N} \tilde{\epsilon}_k(n)\tilde{\epsilon}_{k+1}(n).</math>

Finally, let
: <math>S(N,x) = \sum_{0 \le n < 2^N} \exp(2\pi ixu(n,N)).</math>

Recall that the partition function of the [[Ising model#One dimension|one-dimensional Ising model]] can be defined as follows. Fix <math>N \ge 1</math> representing the number of sites, and fix constants <math>J > 0</math> and <math>H > 0</math> representing the coupling constant and external field strength, respectively. Choose a sequence of weights <math>\eta = (\eta_0,\dots,\eta_{N-1})</math> with each <math>\eta_i \in \{-1,1\}</math>. For any sequence of spins <math>\sigma = (\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_{N-1})</math> with each <math>\sigma_i \in \{-1,1\}</math>, define its Hamiltonian by
: <math>H_{\eta}(\sigma) = -J\sum_{0 \le k < N} \eta_k \sigma_k \sigma_{k+1} - H \sum_{0 \le k < N} \sigma_k.</math>

Let <math>T</math> be a constant representing the temperature, which is allowed to be an arbitrary non-zero [[complex number]], and set <math>\beta = 1/(kT)</math> where <math>k</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]]. The partition function is defined by
: <math>Z_N(\eta,J,H,\beta) = \sum_{\sigma \in \{-1,1\}^N} \exp(-\beta H_{\eta}(\sigma)).</math>

Then we have
: <math>S(N,x) = \exp\left(\frac{\pi iNx}{2}\right)Z_N\left(1,\frac{1}{2},-1,\pi ix\right)</math>
where the weight sequence <math>\eta = (\eta_0,\dots,\eta_{N-1})</math> satisfies <math> \eta_i = 1</math> for all <math>i</math>.<ref>Allouche and Shallit (2003) p. 457–461</ref>
